speakx_0009.instruction: Task 2. Read the announcement, read the student's response, then 30 seconds to prepare and 60 seconds to speak. Summarize the student's OPINION and REASONS - not your own opinion.
speakx_0009.sourceText:
UNIVERSITY ANNOUNCEMENT: Starting next semester, eight small study rooms on the first floor of the library will be combined into a single group work area. The reasons: demand for group space is increasing, and the small rooms are often used by just one person.

STUDENT RESPONSE (written): "I don't think this is a good idea. Those small rooms are the only quiet place left in the evening - the main hall gets loud after six, and I can't do close reading there. And honestly, the reason they gave doesn't match what I see. There's already a group area on the second floor and it's half empty most nights. If group space were really that scarce, that floor would be full."
speakx_0009.sourceNote: ADAPTATION: the original student conversation was in audio form; here it is presented in writing.

speakx_0010.instruction: Task 3. Read the definition, read the lecture, then 30 seconds to prepare and 60 seconds to speak. Explain the term USING examples from the lecture, not the textbook definition.
speakx_0010.sourceText:
READING - Sunk Cost Fallacy: the tendency to continue an endeavor based on what has ALREADY been invested (money, time, effort), rather than on the benefits that can still be gained. Sunk costs cannot be recovered, so logically they are irrelevant to subsequent decisions.

LECTURE (written): "Let me give you two examples. A software company I consulted for had spent four years on a platform. The engineers said plainly that the architecture would not scale. Management approved two more years of funding, and the argument in the meeting was, word for word, 'we've already put four years into this'. That is the fallacy, stated out loud.

A smaller one, from my own life: I once sat through ninety minutes of a terrible film because I had paid for the ticket. The ticket money was gone either way. All I did was add ninety minutes to the loss."
speakx_0010.sourceNote: ADAPTATION: the original lecture was in audio form; here it is presented in writing.

speakx_0011.instruction: Task 4. Read the lecture, then take 20 seconds to prepare and 60 seconds to speak. Summarize TWO main points along with their respective examples.
speakx_0011.sourceText:
LECTURE (written): "Animals facing a cold season have broadly two options, and they cost different things.

The first is migration - leaving before conditions get severe. The Arctic tern is the extreme case: it flies between the Arctic and the Antarctic every year, so it spends most of its life in summer. But look at the price. That is an enormous amount of energy spent on travel alone.

The second option is dormancy - staying, but slowing down. The ground squirrel drops its body temperature close to freezing and its heart rate to a few beats a minute, for months. That saves a remarkable amount of energy. The cost is that it cannot feed at all during that time, so everything depends on what it stored beforehand."
speakx_0011.sourceNote: ADAPTATION: the original lecture was in audio form; here it is presented in writing.

speakx_0017.instruction: Task 4. Read the lecture, then take 20 seconds to prepare and 60 seconds to speak. Summarize TWO main mechanisms along with their respective examples.
speakx_0017.sourceText:
LECTURE (written): "We like to imagine memory as a recording, but it behaves more like a story that is rewritten each time it is told. Let me describe two mechanisms of distortion.

The first is post-event information. What we encounter after an event can be written back into the memory of the event itself. In a classic type of experiment, people watch a short film of a minor car accident. Those later asked how fast the cars were going when they 'smashed' into each other do not just give higher speed estimates than those asked about cars that 'hit' each other - a week later, they are also more likely to remember broken glass that was never in the film. The question has quietly edited the memory.

The second mechanism is imagination inflation. The act of imagining an event leaves a trace that can later be mistaken for the trace of a real experience. In one study, adults who spent a few minutes vividly imagining a childhood incident - breaking a window with their hand - became measurably more confident, weeks later, that it had actually happened to them. Nothing was presented as true; imagining it was enough."
speakx_0017.sourceNote: ADAPTATION: the original lecture was in audio form; here it is presented in writing.
